These topics are absent as distinct lesson records in the supplied Primary 4 Basic Science export. The user has approved a local third-term allocation because NERDC does not prescribe term placement. Lessons are newly authored and are not represented as verbatim source notes.

lessons.title: Safety in Our Environment
objectives: Explain the meaning of safety.
Identify simple ways to keep safe at home, at school and on the road.
Recognise common safety devices and road signs.
Explain why road safety rules should be followed.
lessons.lesson: Safety means taking care to prevent harm to ourselves and other people. At home, keep away from matches, hot stoves, sharp tools and exposed electrical wires. At school, walk rather than run on stairways, follow playground rules and report broken equipment to a teacher. On the road, use a safe crossing point, look carefully in both directions and obey traffic lights and road signs. Safety devices include smoke alarms, fire extinguishers, road signs, traffic lights and protective equipment. Pupils should never try to fight a fire or handle dangerous electrical equipment; they should alert a responsible adult.
examples: Use a zebra crossing where one is available.
Do not touch a damaged electrical cable.
Tell a teacher when a classroom floor is slippery.
lessons.activity: Pupils examine teacher-provided pictures of home, school and road situations. In groups, they identify hazards and suggest a safe action for each. Practise a road-crossing role-play in a safe open area.
evaluation: What is safety?
State two ways to keep safe at home.
Mention two ways to keep safe at school.
Name three road-safety devices or signs.
What should you do if you see a damaged electrical wire?

lessons.title: The Human Body: The Mouth and Its Functions
objectives: Name the main parts of the mouth involved in feeding.
Identify the four main types of teeth.
State the functions of the teeth, tongue and lips.
Describe simple ways to care for the mouth.
lessons.lesson: The mouth helps us eat, speak and begin digestion. The main parts involved in feeding include the teeth, tongue and lips. Incisors at the front help cut food. Canines help tear food. Premolars and molars help crush and grind food. The tongue moves food around the mouth and helps us taste and swallow. The lips help keep food in the mouth and support speech. Saliva moistens food and makes it easier to swallow. Brush teeth gently with a suitable toothbrush and toothpaste, clean the tongue, drink safe water and visit a dental professional when an adult arranges it.
examples: Incisors cut a piece of fruit.
Molars grind food before it is swallowed.
The tongue helps move food while chewing.
lessons.activity: Using a labelled mouth diagram, pupils identify the teeth and match each type to its function. The teacher demonstrates correct tooth-brushing movements with a model or picture.
evaluation: Name the four main types of teeth.
What do incisors do?
State two functions of the tongue.
How do the lips help during feeding?
Give three ways to care for the mouth.

lessons.title: Water Cycle and Formation of Rain
objectives: Explain the water cycle in simple terms.
Describe evaporation and condensation.
Explain how clouds and rain form.
Draw and label a simple water-cycle diagram.
lessons.lesson: The water cycle is the continuous movement of water between the earth and the atmosphere. Heat from the sun causes water in rivers, lakes and wet soil to evaporate and become water vapour. The vapour rises, cools and condenses into tiny water droplets that form clouds. When the droplets join and become heavy, water falls as rain. Rainwater may flow into rivers and lakes or soak into the ground, and the cycle begins again. The sun provides the heat that drives much of this process.
examples: A puddle becomes smaller after sunshine because some water evaporates.
Water droplets can form on the outside of a cold cup because water vapour in the air condenses.
lessons.activity: Pupils observe a teacher-led demonstration of evaporation and condensation using safe equipment. They draw arrows on a simple water-cycle diagram to show evaporation, condensation and rainfall.
evaluation: What is the water cycle?
What causes evaporation?
What happens during condensation?
How is rain formed?
Draw and label a simple water cycle.

lessons.title: Water: Properties, States, Uses and Safe Water
objectives: Describe the observable properties of clean water.
Identify the solid, liquid and gaseous states of water.
Explain evaporation, condensation and freezing using familiar examples.
State common uses of water and ways to protect drinking water.
lessons.lesson: Water is an important natural substance used by people, animals and plants. Clean pure water has no colour, taste or smell. Water can be found in rivers, streams, lakes, wells, rain and underground sources. It is used for drinking, cooking, washing, farming and transport. Water exists in three states: solid ice, liquid water and water vapour, which is a gas. When water is heated, some of it changes into water vapour through evaporation. When water vapour cools, it changes back into tiny liquid drops through condensation. When liquid water becomes very cold, it freezes into ice. These changes do not create a new substance; the material remains water. Water for drinking must be protected from dirt, sewage, chemicals and animal waste. Clear-looking water is not always safe, so drinking water should come from a trusted safe source or be treated appropriately by adults.
examples: Ice melts into liquid water when it warms.
Wet clothes dry because water evaporates into the air.
Water droplets form on the outside of a cold bottle when water vapour in the air cools.
lessons.activity: The teacher displays safe, sealed samples or pictures of ice, liquid water and water vapour. Pupils record the state of water and match each change to melting, freezing, evaporation or condensation. Discuss safe water sources in the community; do not taste unknown samples.
evaluation: State three observable properties of pure water.
Name the three states of water.
What happens to water when it freezes?
Give four uses of water.
Mention three ways drinking water can become contaminated.

lessons.title: Measuring Liquids: Volume and Metric Units
objectives: Explain volume as the amount of space a liquid occupies.
Identify graduated measuring cylinders, cups and jars.
Read a liquid level carefully and record a measurement with its unit.
Use millilitres and litres in simple comparisons.
lessons.lesson: Volume tells us how much space a substance occupies. Liquids take the shape of the container holding them, so we use graduated measuring cylinders, measuring cups or marked jars to find their volume. The metric units commonly used for liquids are millilitres (mL) and litres (L). One litre is equal to 1,000 millilitres. A small medicine cup may hold a few millilitres, while a large bottle may hold one or more litres. To measure accurately, place the container on a flat surface, pour carefully, and read the scale at eye level. For water in a narrow transparent cylinder, read the bottom of the curved surface (the meniscus). Never use medicine measurements for cooking or drink from laboratory equipment. Do not measure fuel, chemicals or unknown liquids in class; use clean water for practice.
examples: A 500 mL bottle contains half a litre.
A 250 mL cup holds less water than a 1 L jug.
lessons.activity: In groups, pupils estimate and then measure clean water using labelled measuring cups or a graduated cylinder. They record each result in mL or L and compare their estimates with the measured values.
evaluation: What is volume?
Name two instruments used to measure liquids.
How many millilitres make one litre?
Why should the scale be read at eye level?
Measure or estimate the capacity of a classroom container and record the unit.
